paras: The Madisonville lynchings were the killing of William "Bill" Bobo and the hanging of Reden S. "Red" Page by a body of several hundred armed citizens at Madisonville, the seat of Madison County, Texas, on January 3, 1888. They also fired on Alf Whitten and warned others to leave, and Governor Ross sent the Navasota Guards. Texas correspondents defended the killings as a rising against a gang of horse and cattle thieves, while a national wire report described "Reformers" killing men who favored saloons.

According to the Fort Worth Gazette's Madisonville correspondent, the county had suffered months of theft, arson, robbery and murder, and men had been killed for serving as state witnesses in theft cases. In November 1887 F. M. Gafford, summoned to testify in a cattle-stealing case, and a man named Keifer were murdered near Madisonville, and Gafford's brother-in-law Peter Peacher was held for the crime.
The night before the killings, Sheriff Black sent the county's jail prisoners to the penitentiary for safekeeping.

On Tuesday, January 3, some 200 or more men met a few miles from Madisonville, formed squads of about thirty, and rode into town armed with shotguns and Winchester rifles. They found Bobo, whom the correspondent called "a man of desperate character," and killed him on the street "in open daylight in the presence of the public" with shots to the head and breast. The squads then went after Whitten, who fled on horseback toward the brush while they fired about twenty shots at him. Finally they took Page from his home to a tree in the nearby woods and hanged him.
Several other men were warned or ordered to leave. The Gazette correspondent named Newton J. Williams, Clay Roberts, Joice Wooley and J. L. Connor as the leaders; the men went unmasked.

Sheriff Black asked Governor Ross for troops, and the governor ordered the Navasota Guards to Madisonville. By January 6 Judge Kittrell thought the trouble over, and the guards entered town unarmed on his advice, though the mob was said to number 500. The militia left after a few days, once the citizens promised the judge to go home and he promised to bring the jailed prisoners before the next district court.

The Madisonville correspondent expected the crowd to surrender and stand trial, but no report of an arrest, inquest, indictment or trial of the lynchers appears in the coverage. In March Governor Ross published a statement recording his "utter condemnation of mob violence" and naming Madison, Wharton and Panola counties. Weeks later, rumors of a ghost at Page's tree drew Sheriff F. M. Black and some twenty-five men to look.

Texas coverage sided with the attackers: the Fort Worth Gazette's first report, headed "Four Men Lynched By an Unmasked Vigilance Committee," said the "best citizens of the county organized themselves into a mob to clean out the set." Its fuller account, headed "NO RANGERS WANTED," called Page "a notorious sneak thief" and concluded that "Public sentiment sustains the conduct of the citizens." The Louisville Courier-Journal's Grimes County correspondent likewise called it "the so-called mob" of men who "do not uphold lynch law."

Outside Texas the story moved in two wires: a Huntsville dispatch about "Reformers" opposed to saloons, printed in the Omaha Bee, the Camden Evening Telegram and elsewhere, and a Navasota dispatch about the militia and the "Bolo gang" of thieves. The Wichita Eagle and the Macon Beacon carried a follow-up putting the dead at "five in all," and Kansas weeklies ran a brief headed "ANARCHY" that reported a second mob forming to lynch the lynchers. Taking the saloon version, the Arizona Weekly Enterprise blamed the "Prohibitionists of Texas" and called their "muscular reformation" out of step with civilization.
Chicago's German-language Illinois Staats-Zeitung ("Richter Lynch") said the mob shot Bobo down "wie einen Hund" but called him a rich horse-thief chief whose friends on juries shielded the gang.

The number of dead varied: the later local reports gave two, wire reports three, the first Gazette dispatch four, and a Navasota follow-up five. Whitten's fate also differed, from "supposedly fatally" shot in the first dispatch to driven out of town in the wire and, in the local account, wounded perhaps but escaped.

reader.title: Madisonville lynchings (1888)
bases: An armed body of several hundred citizens shot William Bobo dead in Madisonville and took Reden S. Page from his home and hanged him from a tree (A1, A11, A22).

Some 200 or more armed citizens acting without legal authority killed Bobo and hanged Page, and the reports justify the killings as a rising against thieves and murderers the courts could not convict (A1, A11, A22).

A Huntsville dispatch (A1), a Madisonville correspondent (A11), a Grimes County correspondent (A22) and the national wires (A2, A3) agree that a citizens' body shot Bobo and hanged Page, though they differ on the total killed.

accounts.label: Local correspondent (Madisonville)
accounts.gist: Two hundred or more of the county's 'best element' killed Bobo and hanged Page after months of crime the courts could not punish; Whitten escaped; public sentiment backed the crowd.

accounts.label: Huntsville dispatch (Texas)
accounts.gist: A mob of 200-300 shot Bobo before the sheriff, hanged Page, shot Whiting and killed one unnamed man; four lynched in all.

accounts.label: Saloon-version wire
accounts.gist: Armed 'Reformers' shot Bolo and hanged Paige and another man; Bolo and his friends favored saloons.

accounts.label: Navasota wire
accounts.gist: Citizens killed Bolo, head of a horse- and cattle-thief gang, and hanged two of his lieutenants during a habeas corpus hearing; a later dispatch put the dead at five.

accounts.label: Grimes County correspondent
accounts.gist: Citizens killed two desperadoes, Boba and Page, ordered others out, then dispersed on the judge's promise of trials for jailed gang members.

framing.detail: Fort Worth Gazette: 'Four Men Lynched By an Unmasked Vigilance Committee' made up of the 'best citizens'; later 'NO RANGERS WANTED' and 'Public sentiment sustains the conduct of the citizens.'
Courier-Journal correspondent: 'The so-called mob' were 'staunch brave men who do not uphold lynch law'.
Northern and western dailies ran the Huntsville and Navasota wires, some headed 'Killed for Favoring Saloons' or 'Horse Thieves in Texas'.
Arizona Weekly Enterprise faulted 'muscular reformation' by Texas prohibitionists; Kansas briefs headed the news 'ANARCHY'.
Illinois Staats-Zeitung ('Richter Lynch') said Bobo was shot down 'wie einen Hund' but described at length his gang's grip on the county's juries.

versions.value: Three (Bobo, Page and an unnamed man; or Bobo and two lieutenants)
